title: Laws of Motion
tagline: Inertia, Newton's three laws, momentum, gravitation and free fall

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Physics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every numerical result in this chapter was independently recomputed by scripts/verify-math.mjs. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: This chapter asks why things move the way they do. The answer begins with inertia, the tendency of a body to keep doing what it is already doing, which is why a force is needed to change any motion at all. Newton's three laws then say how that force is related to mass and acceleration, and the law of conservation of momentum turns those laws into a rule for collisions in which no external force acts. Gravitation closes the chapter by explaining why a body falls, why the value of g is what it is, and why weight and mass are not the same quantity.

facts.label: Newton's laws
facts.value: First: inertia. Second: F = ma. Third: action and reaction are equal and opposite.

facts.label: Momentum
facts.value: p = mv, conserved in a collision when no external force acts

facts.label: Free fall
facts.value: All bodies fall with the same acceleration g = 9.8 m per second squared, whatever their mass

blocks.text: Inertia is the property of a body that resists any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion. It is not a force; it is a property, and it increases with mass. A body continues in its existing state unless a resultant force acts on it, which is exactly what Newton's first law states.

items.meaning: The tendency of a body to resist a change in its state of rest or of uniform motion. It depends on the mass of the body.
The single equivalent force obtained by combining all the forces acting on a body. When it is zero the body is in equilibrium.
The product of mass and velocity, p = mv, measured in kilogram metres per second.

items: Newton's first law: every body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted on by an unbalanced external force.
Inertia is measured by mass; the bigger the mass the greater the inertia.
Momentum is a vector and is conserved in all collisions, whether elastic or inelastic, provided no external force acts.
Impulse is the change of momentum and equals force multiplied by time; impulse equals retarding force times the time for which it acts, which is why cricketers move their hands back while catching.
Action and reaction always act on different bodies, so they never cancel out.

items.text: A body of mass 2 kg is moving at 6 m per second. Find its momentum.
items.note: Momentum is p = mv = 2 x 6 = 12 kg m per second.

learn.title: Newton's second and third laws, F = ma

blocks.text: The second law gives the rate of change of momentum: the acceleration of a body is proportional to the resultant force on it and inversely proportional to its mass, so F = ma. The third law states that to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction, acting on a different body.

items: F = ma, so a = F/m and m = F/a. The newton is defined so that a force of 1 N gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m per second squared.
The unit of momentum is kg m per second, and impulse has the same unit.
Newton's third law pairs are always equal and opposite but act on different bodies, so they never cancel.
A body at constant velocity has zero resultant force and therefore zero acceleration.

items.text: A force of 20 N acts on a body of mass 4 kg. Find its acceleration.
items.note: From a = F/m = 20/4 = 5 m per second squared.

items.text: Two bodies of mass 2 kg and 3 kg moving in the same direction at 4 m per second and 2 m per second collide and stick together. Find their common velocity.
items.note: Total momentum before is 2 x 4 + 3 x 2 = 8 + 6 = 14 kg m per second. Total mass after sticking is 2 + 3 = 5 kg. By conservation of momentum, 14 = 5v, so v = 14/5 = 2.8 m per second in the original direction.

blocks.text: Universal gravitation says that every particle attracts every other particle with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. Near the Earth's surface this attraction gives every body the same acceleration g, which is the striking result that started modern physics.

items: F = G m1 m2 / d squared, where G is 6.67 x 10 to the minus 11 newton metre squared per kilogram squared.
Weight W = mg is a force in newtons; mass in kilograms never changes with location.
A body in free fall accelerates at g = 9.8 m per second squared regardless of its mass, and this is why a feather and a coin fall together in an evacuated tube.
On the Moon, where g is one sixth of its value on Earth, a body weighs one sixth as much but its mass is unchanged.
The value of g decreases with height above the Earth's surface, since the distance from the centre increases.

items.text: Find the weight of a body of mass 5 kg on the Earth and on the Moon, taking g as 9.8 m per second squared and the Moon's g as 1.63 m per second squared.
items.note: On the Earth, W = mg = 5 x 9.8 = 49 N. On the Moon, W = 5 x 1.63 = 8.15 N.

items.text: A body of mass 10 kg is dropped from rest. Taking g as 10 m per second squared, find its velocity after 2 seconds.
items.note: Since it is dropped from rest, u = 0 and a = g = 10 m per second squared. From v = u + at, v = 0 + 10 x 2 = 20 m per second downwards.

learn.title: Action and reaction in everyday life

blocks.text: The third law is easy to state and easy to misuse. The test of a correct action-reaction pair is not that the two forces are equal, but that they act on different bodies. A book resting on a table pushes down on the table and the table pushes up on the book with equal forces, yet the book does not fall, because those two forces act on different objects and cannot cancel.

items: A swimmer pushes the water backwards and the water pushes the swimmer forwards.
A rocket expels gas downwards and is pushed upwards, which works in empty space because no medium is needed.
Friction is necessary for walking; without it the foot would slip and no forward push could be generated.
Action and reaction are always simultaneous; neither can occur without the other.

keyPoints: Inertia is the tendency to resist change of state and it increases with mass.
Newton's first law: a body keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless an unbalanced force acts.
Newton's second law: F = ma, with the newton defined as the force giving 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m per second squared.
Newton's third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction acting on a different body.
Action and reaction never cancel because they act on different bodies.
Momentum p = mv has the unit kg m per second and is a vector.
Momentum is conserved in a collision when no external force acts, and kinetic energy is conserved only in an elastic collision.
Gravitational force F = G m1 m2 / d squared, with G = 6.67 x 10 to the minus 11 N m squared per kg squared.
Weight W = mg is a force in newtons; mass in kilograms does not change with location.
All bodies fall with the same acceleration g = 9.8 m per second squared in free fall, whatever their mass.
The value of g on the Moon is one sixth of its value on the Earth.
Impulse equals the change of momentum and equals force multiplied by time.
examFocus: Momentum questions must state whether the collision is elastic or inelastic, because momentum is conserved in both but kinetic energy only in the elastic case.
In a sticking collision the common velocity is total momentum divided by total mass, which is the form most often needed.
Second law questions should rearrange F = ma to the form asked for rather than multiplying blindly.
For free-fall questions the mass is irrelevant to the motion, so omitting it is correct and not an oversight.
Third-law explanations must explicitly name the two different bodies acted on, or the answer is incomplete.

vocabulary.meaning: The tendency of a body to resist a change in its state of rest or of uniform motion.
The product of mass and velocity, measured in kilogram metres per second.
The change of momentum of a body, equal to force multiplied by the time for which the force acts.
The single force equivalent to all the forces acting on a body.
Motion under gravity alone, in which every body accelerates at g whatever its mass.

questions.prompt: The SI unit of force is:
questions.answer: newton
questions.explanation: Force is measured in newtons, and one newton is the force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m per second squared. The joule is the unit of energy and the watt is the unit of power.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the joule, which is the unit of energy and a common product of force and distance.

questions.prompt: The property of a body that resists a change in its state of motion is:
questions.answer: inertia
questions.explanation: Inertia is the resistance to change of state, and its measure is the mass of the body. Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity and is a different quantity.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing momentum, which combines mass with velocity rather than resisting change on its own.

questions.prompt: Two bodies of mass 4 kg and 6 kg moving in the same direction at 3 m per second and 5 m per second collide and stick. Their common velocity is:
questions.answer: 4.2 m per second
questions.explanation: Total momentum before is 4 x 3 + 6 x 5 = 12 + 30 = 42 kg m per second. Total mass after is 4 + 6 = 10 kg, so by conservation of momentum the common velocity is 42/10 = 4.2 m per second.
questions.commonMistake: Averaging 3 and 5 to get 4 m per second, which would be right only for equal masses.

questions.prompt: The SI unit of momentum is:
questions.answer: kg m per second
questions.explanation: Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity, so its unit is kilogram times metre per second. Newton second has the same dimensions, which is why impulse shares the same unit.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the joule, which is the unit of energy and not of momentum.

questions.prompt: A body of mass 2 kg is acted on by a resultant force of 10 N for 3 seconds. Its change in momentum is:
questions.answer: 30 N s
questions.explanation: The change in momentum equals the impulse, which is force multiplied by time, so 10 x 3 = 30 N s. Equivalently the acceleration is 10/2 = 5 m per second squared and the change in momentum is the mass times the change in velocity, 2 x 5 x 3 = 30 N s.
questions.commonMistake: Dividing the force by the mass to get 5 and calling that the change in momentum, forgetting the factor of time.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: according to Newton's second law, the acceleration of a body is directly proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to its ________.
questions.answer: mass, giving the relation F = ma
questions.explanation: Doubling the mass at the same force halves the acceleration, which is the inverse relationship that defines F = ma.
questions.commonMistake: Saying weight, since mass and weight are related but the second law is written in terms of mass.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in the absence of an external force, the total momentum of a colliding system is ________.
questions.answer: conserved, that is it is the same before and after the collision
questions.explanation: Conservation of momentum is a direct consequence of Newton's third law applied to the two bodies of the collision, and it holds whether or not the collision is elastic.
questions.commonMistake: Saying kinetic energy is conserved, which is true only for an elastic collision.

questions.prompt: State Newton's first law of motion and explain why it cannot be demonstrated directly.
questions.answer: Every body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled by an external unbalanced force to change its state. It cannot be demonstrated directly because in everyday experience no surface is ever completely free of unbalanced forces such as friction and air resistance. A body left on the ground is acted on by friction, and a body moving on a surface is gradually slowed by friction, so the law can only be approximated in the laboratory and not stated as an exact observation.
questions.explanation: The law describes the ideal case of zero resultant force, which real environments never provide exactly.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the law is false because objects eventually stop, when in fact that stopping is caused by friction, which is an external unbalanced force.

questions.prompt: Find the acceleration produced on a body of mass 8 kg by a resultant force of 24 N.
questions.answer: From F = ma, the acceleration is a = F/m = 24/8 = 3 m per second squared.
questions.explanation: The second law is rearranged so that the unknown quantity, the acceleration, is isolated.
questions.commonMistake: Multiplying instead of dividing, which would give 192 m per second squared.

questions.prompt: A body of mass 3 kg moving at 8 m per second collides head on with a stationary body of mass 5 kg, and they move together afterwards. Find their common velocity.
questions.answer: Total momentum before the collision is 3 x 8 + 5 x 0 = 24 kg m per second. Total mass after they stick together is 3 + 5 = 8 kg. By conservation of momentum, 24 = 8v, so v = 3 m per second in the direction of the first body. Kinetic energy is not conserved here: before the collision it is (1/2)(3)(64) = 96 J, and afterwards it is (1/2)(8)(9) = 36 J. The loss of 60 J becomes internal energy, which is what identifies this as an inelastic collision.
questions.explanation: When bodies stick together the masses are simply added and the total momentum divided by the total mass; comparing kinetic energy before and after shows whether the collision was elastic or inelastic.
questions.commonMistake: Treating it as an elastic collision and conserving kinetic energy, which gives an impossible negative value.

questions.prompt: A body of mass 20 kg is pulled by a horizontal force of 50 N on a rough horizontal surface and moves with uniform velocity. Find the frictional force acting and state the coefficient implied if the coefficient is friction divided by the normal reaction.
questions.answer: Since the body moves with uniform velocity, its acceleration is zero, so by Newton's second law the resultant force is zero. The only horizontal forces are the pull of 50 N and friction, which must therefore be 50 N in the opposite direction. The normal reaction balances the weight, so N = mg = 20 x 9.8 = 196 N. The coefficient is friction divided by the normal reaction, which is 50/196 = 0.255.
questions.explanation: Uniform velocity means zero acceleration and therefore zero resultant force, which is the condition that allows friction to be read off directly.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming a moving body has no friction, when in fact friction is precisely what makes uniform velocity possible.

questions.prompt: Find the weight of a body of mass 12 kg on the Earth, taking g as 9.8 m per second squared, and state its mass on the Moon.
questions.answer: On the Earth, W = mg = 12 x 9.8 = 117.6 N. The mass of a body never changes with location, so on the Moon the body still has a mass of 12 kg. Its weight on the Moon would be different, since the Moon's gravitational field is weaker, and would be 12 x 1.63 = 19.56 N using the Moon's value of g.
questions.explanation: Weight depends on the local value of g while mass does not, which is why a body's mass is quoted as the same everywhere.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the mass becomes 12/6 kg on the Moon, confusing weight with mass.

questions.prompt: A ball of mass 0.5 kg is dropped from rest from a height of 44.1 m. Taking g as 9.8 m per second squared, find the time taken to reach the ground and the speed on striking the ground.
questions.answer: Since the ball is dropped from rest, u = 0, a = g = 9.8 m per second squared and s = 44.1 m. Using the second equation, s = ut + (1/2)at squared gives 44.1 = (1/2)(9.8)t squared, so t squared = 44.1 x 2/9.8 = 9, so t = 3 s. Using the first equation, v = u + at = 0 + 9.8 x 3 = 29.4 m per second downwards. Checking with the third equation, v squared = 864.36 and u squared + 2as = 0 + 2 x 9.8 x 44.1 = 864.36, which agrees.
questions.explanation: The mass of the ball does not enter any of the equations, because the acceleration in free fall is the same for every body.
questions.commonMistake: Expecting the 0.5 kg mass to appear somewhere in the calculation, and assuming a lighter ball falls more slowly.

questions.prompt: A book rests on a table. The table pushes up on the book with a force equal and opposite to the force with which the book presses down on the table. Why does the book not fly upwards?
questions.answer: The upthrust from the table and the weight of the book are the two forces that act on the book, and for a book at rest these are equal, so they balance and the resultant force on the book is zero. The equal and opposite pair named in Newton's third law is not this pair: the third law pairs the book's downward push on the table with the table's upward push on the book, and these two forces act on different bodies, the table and the book. Forces acting on different bodies never cancel, which is why they do not produce any motion of the book.
questions.explanation: The confusion is between the balanced forces on the book and the action-reaction pair between the book and the table, which act on different bodies.
questions.commonMistake: Trying to cancel the action and reaction against each other, which is invalid because they act on different objects.

questions.prompt: Explain why a cricketer moves his hands backwards while catching a ball.
questions.answer: The change of momentum of the ball equals the impulse, which is the retarding force multiplied by the time for which it acts. The ball's momentum must be brought from a finite value to zero, and the product of force and time must stay the same for that change to occur. If the hands are held still, the catching force is large because the time is very short, and a large force over a short time is more likely to break the fingers. By drawing the hands back, the time is increased, so the same change of momentum is achieved with a much smaller force spread over a longer interval. The principle is the same reason a heavy truck takes a long distance to stop.
questions.explanation: Impulse is force multiplied by time, so increasing the time allows the same momentum change with a smaller force.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the hands moving back reduces the momentum of the ball, when in fact the momentum change is the same however long it takes.

questions.prompt: Find the momentum of a body of mass 6 kg moving at 4 m per second, and state its SI unit.
questions.answer: Momentum is p = mv = 6 x 4 = 24 kg m per second, and the SI unit is the kilogram metre per second.
questions.explanation: Momentum is simply the product of the mass and the velocity of the body.
questions.commonMistake: Dividing instead of multiplying, which would give a value that is not momentum at all.

questions.prompt: State two situations in which friction is essential for the movement described.
questions.answer: Walking depends on friction, because the foot pushes backwards against the ground and the frictional force from the ground pushes the person forwards; on a frictionless surface the foot would slip and no forward motion could be generated. Braking a vehicle also depends on friction, since the brake pads must exert a frictional force against the wheels to reduce their rotation, and without friction the vehicle would continue at constant speed. In both cases a stationary surface is needed to push against, which is the role of friction.
questions.explanation: Friction is the mechanism by which a body pushes against a fixed surface and is pushed back, which is what allows ordinary motion and stopping.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only one situation when the question asks for two, or choosing an example where friction is being overcome rather than essential.

questions.prompt: A bullet of mass 0.02 kg is fired from a gun and acquires a velocity of 400 m per second in a time of 0.002 s. Find the average force acting on the bullet while it is inside the barrel.
questions.answer: The bullet starts from rest, so its change in velocity is 400 m per second. Its change in momentum is mass times change in velocity, which is 0.02 x 400 = 8 kg m per second. Since this equals the impulse, which is force multiplied by time, the force is 8/0.002 = 4000 N.
questions.explanation: Force is the rate of change of momentum, so dividing the momentum change by the time gives the average force.
questions.commonMistake: Using the mass alone in F = ma without first finding the acceleration over the firing time.

questions.prompt: Why does a body in free fall fall with the same acceleration whatever its mass, and how was this demonstrated?
questions.answer: The gravitational force on a body is proportional to its mass, since F = mg, so doubling the mass doubles the weight. By Newton's second law the acceleration is F/m, so dividing the doubled weight by the doubled mass gives the same acceleration as before. The mass therefore cancels, and every body falls with the same acceleration g = 9.8 m per second squared. Galileo demonstrated this by dropping two spheres of different masses from the same height and showing that, when air resistance was removed by evacuating the tube, they reached the bottom together. In air they do not, because the lighter body has a larger ratio of drag to weight.
questions.explanation: Weight and inertia both scale with mass, so the mass cancels out of the acceleration in F = ma.
questions.commonMistake: Claiming bodies fall together in everyday air, which is only true approximately and fails for very light objects such as feathers.

questions.prompt: A force of 30 N acts on a body of mass 6 kg for 4 seconds from rest. Find the velocity of the body.
questions.answer: The acceleration is a = F/m = 30/6 = 5 m per second squared. Starting from rest, u = 0, so from v = u + at the velocity is 0 + 5 x 4 = 20 m per second in the direction of the force.
questions.explanation: The force must first be converted into an acceleration before the equations of motion can be applied.
questions.commonMistake: Using the force directly in v = u + at in place of the acceleration, which would give 120 m per second.

questions.prompt: State the value of the universal gravitational constant G and the two quantities on which the gravitational force between two bodies depends.
questions.answer: The universal gravitational constant is G = 6.67 x 10 to the minus 11 newton metre squared per kilogram squared. The gravitational force between two bodies is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres.
questions.explanation: G is the constant of proportionality that converts masses and separation into an actual force in newtons.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the force is inversely proportional to the distance rather than to the square of the distance.

questions.prompt: Explain how a rocket can accelerate upwards in empty space, where there is no air for it to push against.
questions.answer: The rocket expels hot gases downwards through its nozzle. By Newton's third law the gases push the rocket upwards with a force equal and opposite to the force with which the rocket pushes the gases down. No medium is required for this, because the reaction partner is the exhaust gas itself, which the rocket carries with it. This is why rockets work in a vacuum, and it is also why a rocket accelerates more efficiently in space, where there is no air resistance opposing the motion.
questions.explanation: The reaction partner is the exhaust the rocket carries, not the surrounding air, so no medium is needed.
questions.commonMistake: Arguing that a rocket cannot work without atmosphere, confusing pushing against air with pushing against its own exhaust.

questions.prompt: Two bodies of mass 3 kg and 5 kg moving in opposite directions at 6 m per second and 4 m per second collide and stick together. Find their common velocity and state its direction.
questions.answer: Take the direction of the 3 kg body as positive. The 3 kg body has momentum 3 x 6 = 18 kg m per second and the 5 kg body has momentum minus 5 x 4 = minus 20 kg m per second. The total momentum is therefore 18 minus 20 = minus 2 kg m per second. The total mass after sticking is 8 kg, so by conservation of momentum the common velocity is minus 2/8 = minus 0.25 m per second. The negative sign shows that the combined body moves in the direction of the original 5 kg body, since that body carried slightly more momentum.
questions.explanation: Opposite directions require opposite signs, and the resultant velocity takes the sign of whichever body had the larger momentum.
questions.commonMistake: Adding the momenta as 18 + 20 = 38, which wrongly treats both bodies as moving the same way.

questions.prompt: Distinguish clearly between the mass and the weight of a body.
questions.answer: Mass is the quantity of matter in a body, measured in kilograms, and it is constant everywhere and is a scalar. Weight is the gravitational force acting on that mass, W = mg, measured in newtons, and it varies with the strength of the gravitational field, so the same body weighs one sixth as much on the Moon as on the Earth. Mass is therefore unchanged by location while weight is changed, and the two are proportional to one another at a given place.
questions.explanation: Mass is a property of the body; weight is a force that depends on both the mass and the local value of g.
questions.commonMistake: Saying a body is weightless on the Moon, when its mass is exactly the same as it was on the Earth.

questions.prompt: A 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m per second is brought to rest in 5 seconds. Find the average retarding force and explain why this force is spread over a longer distance than the same change of speed in 2 seconds.
questions.answer: The change in momentum of the car is 1500 x 20 = 30000 kg m per second, since the final velocity is zero. This equals the impulse, which is force multiplied by time, so the average force is 30000/5 = 6000 N in the direction opposite to the motion. If the car were stopped in 2 seconds instead, the same change of momentum of 30000 kg m per second would have to be produced by a force of 30000/2 = 15000 N, which is two and a half times larger for exactly the same change of speed. A larger force acting for the same overall time produces a larger change of momentum, so achieving the fixed 30000 kg m per second in half the time requires the greater force.
questions.explanation: The momentum change is fixed by the initial and final velocities, so halving the time doubles the force needed.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming the retarding force depends only on the speed, forgetting that it is the rate of change of momentum that fixes it.

questions.prompt: State the forces acting on a body resting on a smooth inclined plane, and explain why such a body cannot stay at rest on its own.
questions.answer: Only two forces act on the body: its weight mg acting vertically downwards, and the normal reaction of the plane acting perpendicular to the surface of the plane. Because the plane is inclined, these two forces are not in the same straight line, so they cannot be equal and opposite and therefore cannot cancel. Resolving the weight along the slope gives a component mg sin(theta) pulling the body down the incline, and since the plane is smooth there is no friction to oppose it. The body therefore slides down the plane. The description of the body being at rest can hold only if it is held by an additional external force, which is a third force not mentioned in the question.
questions.explanation: Weight and normal reaction are not collinear on an incline, so they cannot balance, and a smooth plane supplies no friction to hold the body.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the normal reaction equals the weight on an incline, which is true only for a horizontal surface where the two forces are collinear and vertical.
